label: Assurance of Faith
framing: Assurance does not rest on the strength of your feelings but on the finished work of Christ and the faithfulness of the God who keeps you. Scripture wants you to know, not merely hope, that you belong to him, and it grounds that knowing outside the wavering of your own heart.
cultural: The first readers of John's letters lived in a world of competing teachers, some of whom claimed special knowledge and unsettled ordinary believers about whether they truly had eternal life. John wrote so they might know, anchoring assurance not in secret experience but in a confessed faith in Christ, love for one another, and a changed life, marks any believer could examine.
historical: The Reformation recovered assurance as the birthright of every believer, against a system that had kept people anxious about their standing before God. The Heidelberg Catechism of 1563 opens not with a doctrine but with a comfort, that I am not my own but belong to my faithful Savior. The Puritans, who probed the conscience hard, still pointed the trembling believer away from himself and back to the promise.
application: Rest your assurance on Christ and his promise, not on the temperature of your faith, which rises and falls. Look for the quiet evidences, a faith that confesses Jesus, a love that is learning to forgive, a life slowly turning, rather than demanding a perfect record. Bring your fear to a pastor or mature believer rather than ruling on your own soul alone. And remember the hand that holds you is stronger than the grip you have on it.

verses.text: My sheep listen to My voice; I know them, and they follow Me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand. My Father who has given them to Me is greater than all. No one can snatch them out of My Father’s hand.
verses.where: Jesus says his sheep hear his voice and follow him, that he gives them eternal life, and that no one can snatch them out of his hand or his Father's. The site's plain note says Christians differ on whether a true believer can be lost, and that all sides agree on what the verse most plainly says: the safety of Jesus' sheep rests on his hand and his Father's power, not on their own strength. It adds that many who worry about being lost are the very people still listening for his voice.

verses.text: Everyone the Father gives Me will come to Me, and the one who comes to Me I will never drive away.
verses.where: Jesus says that the one who comes to him he will never drive away. The site's note says Christians read the first half of the verse, about the Father's giving, in different ways, and that every tradition reads the second half as an unqualified welcome. Its plain note says he does not promise to check whether you were chosen; he promises not to drive you away.

verses.text: For you did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but you received the Spirit of sonship, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!” The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children.
verses.where: Paul tells believers they did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns them to fear, but the Spirit by whom they cry, Abba, Father. The site's note says the Spirit's witness is the ground of Christian assurance, and that Christian traditions describe that witness in different ways. Its plain note asks what fear still drives your relationship with God.

verses.text: For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
verses.where: The chapter that began with no condemnation ends with no separation: Paul names every power that might threaten and denies that any of them can separate believers from God's love in Christ. The site's plain note says churches answer differently whether a believer can turn away, and that if you are afraid you have lost God's love, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has fallen away.

verses.text: I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life.
verses.where: John says plainly why he wrote: so that those who believe in the name of the Son of God may know that they have eternal life. The site's plain note says Christian traditions explain assurance differently, and that all of them read John as writing to give confidence, not fear, and ground it in Christ, not in the strength of our feelings.

verses.text: Immediately the boy’s father cried out, “I do believe; help my unbelief!”
verses.where: A desperate father, asked about his faith, cries out that he does believe, and asks Jesus to help his unbelief. The site's note says his prayer shows that faith and doubt can live in one person, that faith includes asking for more faith, and that Jesus heals in response to this mixed confession. You do not need perfect faith to come.

verses.text: But when he saw the strength of the wind, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, cried out, “Lord, save me!” Immediately Jesus reached out His hand and took hold of Peter. “You of little faith,” He said, “why did you doubt?”
verses.where: Peter steps out of the boat at Jesus' word, sees the wind, begins to sink and cries, Lord, save me. The site's note says Jesus calls him little faith, not no faith, and that the rescue comes before the rebuke. Its plain note says the point of the story is not Peter's power but Jesus' hand.

verses.text: Then he said, “Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom!” And Jesus said to him, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.”
verses.where: A criminal dying beside Jesus asks only to be remembered when Jesus comes into his kingdom, and Jesus answers, today you will be with me in Paradise. The site's note says his faith had no evidence to lean on but the manner of Jesus' dying, and that his salvation came without baptism, good works, or time to reform. The plain note says that if you think it is too late for you, this story is for you.

verses.text: being confident of this, that He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus.
verses.where: Paul writes from prison to friends he thanks God for every time he remembers them, confident that the one who began a good work in them will carry it on to completion. The confidence is in what God has begun, not in how well the Philippians are doing.

verses.text: For this reason, even though I suffer as I do, I am not ashamed; for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day.
verses.where: Near the end of his life, suffering for the gospel, Paul says he is not ashamed, because he knows whom he has believed and is convinced that he is able to guard what Paul has entrusted to him. The site's plain note asks whether your confidence rests on what you know about God or on knowing him.

links.label: Practical guides for the inner life

misread.taken: “Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith” is taken as a command to search the heart again and again for proof of being truly saved, so that a believer keeps checking and never finds enough.
misread.says: The site's notes say to read the verse in its setting. Some in Corinth were testing Paul, asking whether Christ really spoke through him, and Paul turns the test back on them, expecting them to pass: can't you see for yourselves that Jesus Christ is in you? The test is whether Christ is present, not whether a life is flawless. Healthy self-examination looks first to Christ, not to one's own record, and leads to confidence, not despair.
misread.text: Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Can’t you see for yourselves that Jesus Christ is in you—unless you actually fail the test?

misread.taken: “I never knew you” is heard by sincere, anxious believers as a warning aimed at them, so that no amount of faith or service can ever be sure it is enough.
misread.says: The site's plain note says this passage has frightened many sincere people, and that Christian traditions answer the question of assurance in different ways. It points out two things they share. The people Jesus turns away rest their whole case on their own works and never mention mercy, and his answer is not anxious self-examination but hearing his words and doing them, words that began with mercy for the poor in spirit. If you are afraid you are one of the people in this verse, the note says, that fear is itself a sign that you care what Jesus thinks.
misread.text: Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only he who does the will of My Father in heaven. Many will say to Me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in Your name, and in Your name drive out demons and perform many miracles?’ Then I will tell them plainly, ‘I never knew you; depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness!’

whole: If the fear of being lost has taken your sleep, or has come with thoughts of hurting yourself, please tell someone you trust today; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Some people doubt they were ever really saved because they cannot remember a moment of conversion, or because they prayed a prayer as a child and are not sure it counted. Some fear they have sinned too often, or too badly, since coming to faith. Some lie awake checking their hearts for proof and never find enough. And some have heard preaching that made them wonder whether they are among those Jesus says he never knew.

Behind much of this is a quiet shift in where assurance is looked for: away from Christ and onto the strength of our feelings, the sincerity of a prayer, or the record of the week. The site's note on 1 John 5 says that every Christian tradition reads John as writing to give confidence, not fear, and grounds that confidence in Christ, not in the strength of our feelings. Scripture's people believed with mixed hearts. A father cried that he believed and asked for help with his unbelief, and Jesus healed his son; Peter sank, and Jesus' hand came before his question. The note on Romans 8 says the fear of having lost God's love is not usually the mark of someone who has.

So look first to Christ, not to your own record. Read the promises as they are given: the one who comes to Jesus he will never drive away; no one can snatch his sheep out of his hand or his Father's; nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God in Christ. When you cannot find your own prayer, let the Spirit's cry, Abba, Father, be yours. Where a sin needs confessing, confess it, and then believe the forgiveness. Where the checking has become a loop the mind cannot leave, talk with a pastor or a friend you trust; the notes say such fear can be part of anxiety or a habit of the mind, and a counselor can help too. Faithful churches describe assurance in different ways, set out below, and all of them send the anxious to Christ.

The hope here is not a feeling you must keep alive but a person who keeps his word. Paul knew whom he had believed, and was sure that the one who began a good work would carry it to completion. A dying criminal with nothing to show asked only to be remembered, and Jesus answered, today. John wrote so that those who believe may know they have eternal life. Your safety rests on his hand, not on the strength of yours.

differ.share: Christians agree that salvation is God's gift in Christ, received by faith, that John wrote so that believers may know they have eternal life, and that the safety of Jesus' sheep rests on his hand and his Father's power, not on their own strength.

views.name: Kept to the end
views.body: Many Reformed and Calvinist churches, and much of the Baptist world, teach the perseverance of the saints: those God has truly called will be kept by him and cannot finally be lost. They hear that promise in John 10 and Romans 8, and hold that assurance grows through God's promises, the Spirit's witness and the fruit of grace, though it may be clouded for a time.

views.name: Faith can be abandoned
views.body: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Wesleyan and Methodist churches, and many others, teach that a believer can fall away, noting that the promise is given to sheep who keep listening and following and pointing to warnings such as Hebrews 6:4-6 and John 15:6. Wesleyans stress the Spirit's direct witness that believers are God's children, Lutherans point the troubled to Christ in the preached word and the sacraments, and Catholic teaching speaks of firm hope in God's mercy while holding that no one can know with complete certainty, without a special revelation, that he will persevere to the end.

differ.after: The creeds do not settle this, and the site's notes on John 10, Romans 8 and 1 John 5 set out these views without choosing. Both, rightly held, lead to the same place: a humble clinging to Christ, not careless presumption and not gnawing fear.

deep.sit: Where have you been looking for proof that you belong to God, and what would change if you looked first at the one who said he would never drive away anyone who comes?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says God knows the worst about you and has not let go, and that if you have felt too far gone you should read these verses slowly: there is no place where his hand cannot reach you.
prayer.text: Where can I go to escape Your Spirit? Where can I flee from Your presence? If I ascend to the heavens, You are there; if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there. If I rise on the wings of the dawn, if I settle by the farthest sea, even there Your hand will guide me; Your right hand will hold me fast.

careLines.text: Such fear can be part of anxiety or a habit of the mind, and that is not a failure of faith.
Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust, and if the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
